This is a sample project notebook. It shows one way to tell a project's story:
start with a question, make the experiment reproducible, and keep a place for
the questions that remain.

## The question

A cellular automaton is a world built from a grid and a local update rule.
Each cell can be alive or empty. It sees only its eight nearest neighbors,
yet the whole grid can develop patterns that persist, oscillate, or move.

What would we need to record to distinguish those behaviors in a small,
controlled experiment?

## One rule, many behaviors

For this example, the update rule is Conway's Game of Life:

- A live cell survives with two or three live neighbors.
- An empty cell becomes alive with exactly three live neighbors.
- All other cells become empty.

Every cell updates at the same time. There is no additional instruction
for a pattern to move or repeat; those behaviors emerge from the rule.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="The central observation"}
Counting live cells is not enough to describe a pattern. A stationary block,
an oscillating blinker, and a moving glider all keep their population after
each complete cycle, while their spatial behavior differs.
:::

## From an idea to a notebook

The [experiment](experiment.qmd) follows three small seeds for eight steps.
It includes a compact Python implementation and a table that can be checked
without a dataset or a large compute environment.

The [notes](notes.qmd) collect the limits of the experiment and possible
next steps. This separation leaves room for an idea to grow into several
pages while keeping the overview easy to read.
